findings.analytical_note: Noble opponents of Gustavus’s own policies killed him; attribution to Jacobinism by king and plotters nevertheless reinforced the image of French hostility to monarchy.
Population, volunteering, surviving professional soldiers, NCO advancement and relatively intact artillery qualify any account of victories resting only on revolutionary enthusiasm.

Russian conquest of Poland and Prussia’s ambitions distracted the coalition during French successes. The second partition subsequently freed attention for renewed western action, despite excluding and angering Austria.

Aid to foreign peoples became linked to abolition of old institutions, exclusion of their supporters, and compulsory support of French armies. Liberating language and fiscal exploitation require distinct access.

Some local groups first requested annexation, while Belgian exiles and Dumouriez wanted a separate state. French natural-frontier ambitions widened war; later plebiscite majorities came from tiny participating minorities.

Britain initially avoided war despite hostility to revolution. Belgian occupation, opening the Scheldt, threats to the Dutch settlement and regicide combined strategic and political causes; loyalist organization outweighed corresponding societies.
British diplomacy assembled a broad coalition without a general binding treaty; states’ participation and motives differed.

reader_access_routes: Dumouriez: treason and failed march on Paris
findings.analytical_note: Defeat and soldiers’ refusal to march on Paris led Dumouriez to defect. French withdrawal of open-ended international aid and peace overtures were read as weakness rather than moderation.

Expanded enemies and commitments met shrinking forces as single-campaign volunteers went home. Treason fears and executions of generals discouraged risk; internal rebellion compounded frontier reverses.
The allies failed to exploit French weakness because coordination was poor and territorial, colonial and eastern aims competed with restoring monarchy. Russia withheld troops without subsidy.

Early recovery preceded the full effect of mass mobilization. February conscription met resistance; August requisition mobilized military-age single men plus labor, transport, buildings and materials throughout society.
Amalgamation sought equal organization, pay and equipment across line, Guard and volunteer forces. Adoption was gradual, extending well beyond the original 1793 decree.

Improvised extraction and manufacture supported unprecedented manpower; French districts bore costs before renewed conquest. Mass attacks and citizen commitment changed tactics and ferocity, without implying instantly perfected administration.

reader_access_routes: Glorious First of June: convoy objective
findings.analytical_note: Fleurus was the decisive turning point. Naval battle losses must be distinguished from success in protecting the grain convoy; technical and organizational contributions merit access alongside named victories.

Polish revolution drew inspiration but little material aid from France. Kosciuszko’s peasant concessions aimed at mass mobilization, while noble allies were divided; military timing was forced by Russian army reduction.
Crushing the rising produced mass killing and final partition; rival partitioning powers and possible inter-allied war helped induce Prussian peace with France.
Montagnard policy prioritized securing the Revolution inside France, despite Polish sympathies and the benefit Poland conferred by diverting enemies. Aid was reconsidered too late.

Frozen rivers, French advance and British retreat helped patriot takeovers. Dutch expectations of autonomy met indemnity, loan, territorial concessions, occupation costs and imposed alliance; this concrete gap warrants separate retrieval.

Prussian peace left the Rhineland exposed to France. Spanish popular resistance contrasted with court fear of subversion; conciliatory French terms freed troops for other fronts, and colonial gains had limited immediate use.
The conspirators’ inspiration was chiefly reforming Habsburg rulers rather than imitation of France. Government fright accelerated abandonment of reforms they hoped to protect.

Renewed Belgian annexation sustained Austrian and British resistance. British Caribbean ambitions combined planter protection, suppression of slave rebellion and commerce; costly expeditions did not subdue Guadeloupe or Saint-Domingue.

Renewed reform agitation met repression; Irish Catholics initially received limited concessions. Jury acquittals prompted statutory restrictions rather than proving reformers’ guilt; Scottish transportation and Irish bans differ from English proceedings.

Tone’s nonsectarian reform network and exile advocacy promoted intervention. Hoche’s rivalry and French desire to reciprocate subversion aided plans; weather defeated the expedition, and Doyle doubts that landing at that place and time would have produced the promised rising.

The intended diversion became the principal theater. Bonaparte’s speed, repeated Austrian relief efforts, stretched communications and eventual reinforcements qualify a simple uninterrupted triumph narrative.

Bonaparte imposed unauthorized peace and state-building, using neutral Venice as compensation and preserving the pope against expectations in Paris. Personal military authority displaced civilian war aims.
Invasion anxiety and lending strain prompted a bank run. Naval mutineers sought conditions and pay; the text reports no serious evidence of subversion, and subsequent victories restored confidence.

Purge of moderates hardened negotiations. Campo Formio recognized French gains and sister republics but could not bind the Empire over the Rhine; British willingness to concede European conquests still fell short of French demands for colonial restitution.

reader_access_routes: War: cause of radicalization and terror
findings.analytical_note: Barruel systematized an anti-Christian masonic conspiracy account that drove repression of lodges. Doyle explicitly rejects this causal account and attributes much revolutionary violence to war; preserve attribution and rebuttal, not just the allegation.

qualifications: p. 215 dates creation of the Cispadane Republic to December 1796 but its absorption into the Cisalpine to June 1796; record as an internal sequence/date anomaly without external correction.
The chapter’s treatment of French policy toward Polish insurgents is critical of the gap between rhetorical fraternity and practical assistance.
